title: How do consumer goods companies make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Consumer goods (FMCG) economics for case interviews: brands, retailers as customers, distribution, promotions, private label and new product launches.
hook: Consumer goods companies make the products on supermarket shelves: snacks, shampoo, drinks. Their cases revolve around brands, getting onto shelves, and the push and pull with retailers who also sell their own cheaper brands.
body:
How they make money

They sell to retailers, who sell to shoppers. Revenue depends on distribution (how many stores stock the product), rate of sale (how fast it sells in each store) and price.

A worked example: distribution versus rate of sale

A snack is in 5,000 stores, each selling 20 packs a week at £1.50 to the retailer: £7.8M a year (5,000 × 20 × £1.50 × 52). Getting into 1,000 more stores adds about £1.6M. Raising sales per store from 20 to 24 packs adds about the same. Which is cheaper to achieve decides the strategy.

The tensions

  • Promotions lift volume but can train shoppers to buy only on deal.
  • Private label: retailers' own brands compete on the same shelf.
  • Retailer power: a few large supermarkets often control a large share of sales.

Typical consumer goods case questions

  • How should we launch a high-protein snack?
  • Why has our market share fallen?
  • Should we cut back on promotions?

Distribution can matter more than the headline price

A snack brand sells through 5,000 stores. Each store sells 20 packs a week, and the manufacturer receives £1.20 per pack after retailer margins. Annual manufacturer revenue is approximately 5,000 × 20 × 52 × £1.20 = £6.24 million. If distribution grows to 7,000 stores but sales per store fall to 16 packs a week, annual revenue rises to about £6.99 million, only 12% higher despite 40% more stores. That is why both distribution breadth and rate of sale matter.

In a category-growth case, distinguish sales into the retailer from purchases by final consumers. A one-time pipeline fill can inflate shipments without sustainable consumer demand. Promotions may boost short-term volumes while encouraging customers to delay purchases until discounts return. Your analysis should include trade spending, returns and inventory at distributors.

Assume a manufacturer earns £0.40 contribution on each of 5.2 million annual packs. A packaging redesign saves 5p per pack and costs £150,000 to implement. The gross annual saving is £260,000, so simple payback is roughly seven months, if volume and quality are unchanged. But a cheaper package that makes the product less noticeable or damages it in transit may wipe out the saving.

When a consumer-goods client loses market share, break the issue into stores stocking the product, shelf availability, shoppers choosing the brand, frequency of purchase and average price. Decide which stage to investigate using observed changes, not a standard marketing checklist.
